name: Watt separate-condenser engine arrangement
summary: Watt's steam engine design in which steam is condensed in a separate vessel, so the working cylinder stays hot and much less fuel is wasted.
description: Watt’s steam-engine arrangement in which steam is condensed in a vessel separate from the working cylinder; the surviving second 1765 model is an early physical witness.
tier_reason: The scoped record is a particular configuration, local witness, trial or material application. Dependence across fields or generations on THIS referent is not established; do not inherit the importance of its broader missing family.

impact.note: An improvement so large that steam power was reorganised around it across Britain, Europe and America; the Watt engine line grew from it.

why: According to Watt’s later recollections and historical accounts, investigation of a troublesome Newcomen model led him to consider the heat lost in repeatedly cooling and reheating the working cylinder.

date.basis: Museum attribution of surviving object 1876-1267; this is a model date, not industrial operation.

events.statement: Watt's surviving second cylinder-and-separate-condenser model; condensation occurs outside the working cylinder.
events.caveats: Formerly misidentified as the first model. The museum describes alterations and probable sealing difficulties; reliable prolonged operation is not claimed.

evidence.supports: Maker, Glasgow attribution, 1765 date and separate-condenser arrangement.

date.label: by 11 March 1776
date.basis: The 11 March 1776 report says the engine had been set to work on the preceding Friday.

events.statement: A separate-condenser Watt engine was set to work pumping at Bloomfield Colliery in the presence of the colliery proprietors and other witnesses by 11 March 1776.
events.scope: A Watt steam pumping engine with a separate condenser and a 50-inch working cylinder; the surviving second 1765 model is a witness to an earlier version of the arrangement, not this deployed engine.
events.caveats: This concerns the deployed Bloomfield engine, not operation of the surviving second model. The original newspaper issue was not separately inspected; Langford’s 1868 printed transcription was inspected. No first commercial offer or universal uptake is asserted.

evidence.supports: Reports an operating 50-inch Watt engine with a condenser at Bloomfield Colliery in the presence of its proprietors and other witnesses; the original Gazette was not independently inspected.

evidence.locator: Printed pp. 11–12 and 15, on the separate condenser and Bloomfield engine
evidence.supports: Explains the separate condensing vessel in Watt’s engine and identifies the Bloomfield engine as the full-size realization.

earliest_record.rationale: Earliest defensible dated record of this scoped referent in the retained evidence; later community entry is recorded separately. Museum attribution of surviving object 1876-1267; this is a model date, not industrial operation. Formerly misidentified as the first model. The museum describes alterations and probable sealing difficulties; reliable prolonged operation is not claimed. This is the earliest supported record currently established here, not certification of absolute priority.

community_entry.rationale: A working engine in the colliery supplies direct historical use of the refined configuration class; the surviving model documents an earlier experimental witness.
community_entry.caveats: This concerns the deployed Bloomfield engine, not operation of the surviving second model. The original newspaper issue was not separately inspected; Langford’s 1868 printed transcription was inspected. No first commercial offer or universal uptake is asserted.

caveats: This configuration-class record includes the surviving 1765 model and the different Bloomfield customer engine as scoped witnesses. The 1769 patent specification is documentary; neither physical identity nor first deployment of the model is implied. The Gazette issue and original cylinder order were not independently inspected.

links.statement: Did Watt’s investigation of a Newcomen model lead to his development of separate condensation?
links.scope: Historical development of the separate-condenser arrangement, rather than attachment of a condenser to the Glasgow Newcomen model.
links.caveats: The Glasgow account also draws on Watt’s recollection; the University states there is no evidence a separate condenser was attached to its Newcomen model. The historical development link awaits independently informative corroboration.

evidence.supports: Retrospective account of Watt’s work on the Newcomen model, heat loss and development of separate condensation; includes recollections attributed to Watt.

evidence.locator: James Watt and the University of Glasgow, paragraphs on model repair and separate condenser
evidence.supports: University account connects work on its model with investigation of heat loss and the separate condenser; notes no evidence that the condenser was attached to that model.

evidence.locator: Paragraphs beginning “The separate condenser resolved” and “By condensing the steam”
evidence.supports: Independent museum explanation of the technical problem of cylinder cooling and separate condensation.

links.finding: Watt’s retrospective recollection and later accounts associate the Newcomen model with the development; the independent museum source explains the technical mechanism but does not independently corroborate that historical sequence.
